slides.title: Miscellaneous Commands
slides.body:
Miscellaneous Commands
Package Management
sudo, su, chown, chmod
apt, yum, brew
Super User and File Permissions
slides.notes:
In today’s session, we’re going to dive into some very important topics.
First, we’ll look at sudo, su, chown, and chmod — these are powerful commands related to super user access and file permissions.
And then, we’ll wrap up with package management, learning how tools like apt, yum, and brew make installing and managing software much easier.

slides.title: Super User & File Permissions
slides.notes: Alright, moving forward — let’s talk about Super User and File Permissions

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
Linux Users
The root user, also known as the superuser or administrator,  has access to all commands and files
Admin
slides.notes:
Now, let’s look at Linux users.
At the top, we have the root user, also called the superuser or administrator. This user has full access to all commands and files in the system — nothing is restricted.
Alongside root, we also have admin users, who can perform elevated tasks when needed, usually with the help of sudo.

slides.title: Linux Users
slides.body:
Root User
.sudo. command temporarily elevates the privileges allowing users to complete sensitive tasks without logging in as the root user
“Super User do”
$ sudo command
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo.
slides.notes:
now let’s talk about the root user. Sometimes, we need special permissions to perform sensitive tasks, like installing software or changing system files. Instead of logging in as root directly, we use the sudo command.
sudo stands for ‘Super User Do’, and it temporarily grants  privileges to complete the task.

slides.title: Linux Commands
slides.body:
Executable Path
.which. command is used to identify the location of a given executable path
$ which command
Syntax
$  which sudo
/usr/bin/sudo
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which.
slides.notes:
Now, moving ahead, let’s talk about the which command. This command helps us find the location of an executable in the system. For example, when we run which sudo, it shows /usr/bin/sudo, meaning that’s the path where the sudo program is stored.
This is really useful when you want to know where exactly a command is coming from, especially if multiple versions are installed on your system.

slides.title: Linux Commands
slides.body:
Create New Users
. useradd . is used to create a new user with the given username 
$ sudo useradd username
Syntax
$  sudo useradd rahul
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd.
slides.notes:
Next, we’ll look at how to create new users in Linux.
For this, we use the useradd command. It takes a username as input and creates a new user on the system. Since it’s an administrative task, we run it with sudo.

For example, sudo useradd rahul  creates a new user named rahul.

slides.title: Linux Commands
slides.body:
Set/Change User Password
. passwd . is used to set or change password of a given user
$ sudo passwd username
Syntax
$ sudo passwd rahul
New password:
Retype new password:
passwd: password updated successfully
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd.
slides.notes:
Moving ahead, once a user is created, we need to set or update their password. For this, Linux provides the passwd command. Using sudo passwd username, we can assign or reset a password for that user.
In the example, sudo passwd rahul  prompts us to enter and confirm the new password, and then shows “password updated successfully”.
So now, in addition to sudo, which, and useradd, we’ve also learned how to manage user passwords with passwd.

Practical

slides.title: Linux Commands
slides.body:
Execute Command as Another User
. su . is used to execute command as another user 
$ su -c command user
Syntax
$ su user
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su.
slides.notes:
Next, let’s look at how we can execute commands as another user. The command for this is su.
We can either switch directly to another user with su username, or run a specific command as that user using su -c "command" username.
This is especially useful when you want to test or run something under a different user’s environment without logging out.

slides.title: File Permissions
slides.body:
Authorization Levels
Multi-user operating systems like linux provide two levels of authorization in securing the files
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su.
slides.notes:
Moving on, let’s talk about file permissions in Linux. Since Linux is a multi-user operating system, security becomes very important. That’s why it provides two levels of authorization to protect files:
Permission → defines what actions (read, write, execute) a user can perform on a file.
Ownership → defines who owns the file and controls its access.
This forms the basis of Linux security. Without proper permissions and ownership, multiple users working on the same system would face risks.

slides.title: File Permissions
slides.body:
User Ownership
Users accessing a file/ directory can be categorized into 3 types
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su.
slides.notes:
Moving ahead, let’s understand how Linux categorizes who can access a file or directory. There are three types of users:
Owner → usually the creator of the file, with primary control over it.
Group → a set of users grouped together, all sharing the same level of access.
Others → any remaining users on the system who are neither the owner nor part of the group.
This separation ensures that permissions can be managed in a very controlled way. For example, a project file might be fully editable by the owner, accessible by the team (group), but only viewable or even hidden from everyone else.
So far, we’ve been learning important commands like sudo, which, useradd, passwd, and su. Now we’re tying them to file access rules through ownership.
tables: User who is considered as owner
A group of users, who are assigned a specific permission
Any other users who doesn’t belong to the above two types

Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su.

slides.notes:
Next, let’s combine ownership with the actual permissions a file can have. In Linux, permissions are divided into three actions:
Read (r) → allows opening and reading the file.
Write (w) → allows modifying the contents.
Execute (x) → gives the right to run the file as a program or script.
And remember, these permissions are set separately for three categories of users: owner, group, and others.
So, a file can have different levels of access depending on who is trying to use it. For example, the owner may have full access, while others might only be able to read it.

slides.title: File Permissions
slides.body:
File Permissions in Linux
$ ls -l
$ drwxrwxr-x  2 ib-developer ib-developer  4096 Mar 22 16:42  images
$ -rw-rw-rwx  1 ib-developer ib-developer  0 Mar 23 10:26  sample.txt
Bash
file
directory
user
group
others
r  -  read 
w - write 
x  - execute
-    no permission
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su.
slides.notes:
Next, let’s look at how permissions actually appear in Linux. When we run the command ls -l, it displays files and directories along with their permissions.
For example:
drwxrwxr-x → here, the first letter d means it’s a directory, while - would mean it’s a file.
The next three characters rwx → permissions for the user (owner).
The following three rwx → permissions for the group.
The last three r-x → permissions for others.
In short:
r → read,
w → write,
x → execute,
and - means no permission.
So, by reading this code, you can immediately know who can read, edit, or execute a file.
Quick check for you: Looking at -rw-rw-rwx, can you tell me which users have full permissions here?

slides.title: File Permissions
slides.body:
Changing Permissions
$ chmod permissions filename
Syntax
"chmod"  stands for change mode
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su. .chmod.  
$ chmod 702 sample.txt
Bash
slides.notes:
Now, we will be learning about how to change file permissions using the chmod command. The syntax is simple:
chmod permissions filename

Here, permissions is a 3-digit number, and filename is the file you want to change.
Now, let’s break this down.
The first digit represents permissions for the user (the owner of the file).
The second digit represents permissions for the group.
The third digit represents permissions for others (everyone else).
So for example, if the number is 702:
7 is for the user,
0 is for the group,
2 is for others.
Now, how do we decide what number to put? Each number corresponds to a combination of permissions:
0 means no permissions → symbol is ---. The user cannot read, write, or execute.
1 means execute only → symbol is --x.
2 means write only → symbol is -w-.
3 means write + execute → symbol is -wx.
4 means read only → symbol is r--.
5 means read + execute → symbol is r-x.
6 means read + write → symbol is rw-.
7 means read + write + execute → symbol is rwx.
So when we use chmod, we’re basically giving a code that tells Linux which permissions should apply.
Now, notice there’s also a binary column in the table. Why is that there?
Permissions are actually stored in binary at the system level:
So for example when we write 5 it will be represented as “101”, so let's break it down …..2*0 *1 + 2*1 * 0 + 2*1 * 2 = 5So you understood this right ?

slides.title: File Permissions
slides.body:
Changing Permissions
7 - read, write and execute
6 - read and write
4 - only read
$ chmod 764 sample.txt
$ ls -l
$ -rwxrw-r--  1 ib-developer cdrom            0 Mar 23 10:26  sample.txt
Bash
user
group
others
7 6 4
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su. .chmod.
slides.notes:
Moving ahead, let’s see an example of changing file permissions with chmod.
Here, I’ve run chmod 764 sample.txt.
The number 7 applies to the user → it gives full permissions: read, write, and execute.
The number 6 applies to the group → which means read and write only.
The number 4 applies to others → which allows only read.
When we check with ls -l, you can see it reflected as -rwxrw-r--. This tells us that the owner has all rights, the group can only read and write, and others can just read.Practical
👉 Quick check for you: if I had used chmod 700 sample.txt, what would happen for group and others?

slides.title: File Permissions
slides.body:
Changing Ownership
For changing the user of a file/directory
$ sudo chown root sample.txt
$ ls -l$ -rwxrw-r--  1 root cdrom            0 Mar 23 10:26  sample.txt
Bash
$ sudo chown user filename
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su. .chmod. .chown.
slides.notes:
Next, let’s look at how we can change the ownership of a file.
By default, when a file is created, the user who created it becomes the owner. But sometimes, we may want to transfer ownership—like assigning it to the root user.
For this, we use the chown command.
In the example, sudo chown root sample.txt changes the owner of sample.txt to root.
When we check with ls -l, notice that the owner now shows as root instead of the original user.
Practical

👉 Question for you: Why do you think changing ownership might be necessary in a multi-user system?

slides.title: File Permissions
slides.body:
Changing Ownership
For changing the user and group of a file/directory
$ sudo chown root:root sample.txt
$ ls -l$ -rwxrw-r--  1 root root           0 Mar 23 10:26  sample.txt
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  sudo. .which. .useradd. .passwd. .su. .chmod. .chown. 
$ sudo chown user:group filename
Syntax
slides.notes:
Moving ahead, we can also change both the user and the group that own a file.
The syntax for this is: sudo chown user:group filename
For example, in the command sudo chown root:root sample.txt, we are setting both the user and the group of sample.txt to root.
When we run ls -l after this, notice how the ownership now shows root root — meaning both the user and group are assigned to root.

Practical

slides.title: Packaging
slides.body:
Packaging Tool
$ sudo apt
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.
APT stands for the Advanced Packaging Tool
It is used to install, upgrade or remove software packages in linux
slides.notes:
Next, let’s talk about the APT tool, which stands for Advanced Packaging Tool.
This is the default package manager in Debian-based systems like Ubuntu. With APT, we can install new software, upgrade existing ones, or even remove packages completely.
The basic syntax starts with sudo apt, followed by the action you want — for example, installing or updating a package.
So whenever you’re working on Ubuntu and need new software, APT is your go-to command.

slides.title: Packaging
slides.body:
Installing Package
Installing a package from a repository
$ sudo apt install package_name
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.
slides.notes:
Moving on, let’s see how we can actually install a package using APT.
The command is simple: sudo apt install package_name
Here, you just replace package_name with the actual software you want to install. For example, if you wanted to install Python, you’d type sudo apt install python3.
This command will fetch the package from the repository and set it up on your system. Very straightforward, right?

slides.title: Packaging
slides.body:
Package Managers
$ yum install firefox
$ brew install firefox
Mac OSX
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.  brew. .yum.
slides.notes: Moving on, let’s talk about package managers.They help us install or update software with a single command. For example,On Mac, we use brew install firefoxWhereas,On Debian-based Linux, we might use apt install firefox, while on RHEL-based Linux, it’s yum install firefox.Much easier than downloading files manually, right?

slides.title: Web Content
slides.body:
Downloading Files From Web
.wget. is a command-line utility for downloading files from the web
$ sudo apt install wget 
Syntax
$ sudo brew install wget 
Syntax
$ sudo yum install wget 
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.  brew. .yum. .wget.
slides.notes:
Moving ahead, let’s see how we can download files from the web directly from the terminal.
The command we use is wget, which is a utility that helps us fetch files from the internet.
Before using it, we need to make sure it’s installed. Depending on your system:
On Ubuntu/Debian, run sudo apt install wget.
On MacOS, use sudo brew install wget.
On CentOS/RHEL, run sudo yum install wget.
So once installed, wget can grab files right from a given URL. Pretty useful when you don’t want to open a browser.

slides.title: Web Content
slides.body:
Downloading Files From Web
$ wget "URL" 
Syntax
ib-developer@cloud:~$ wget "https://www.example.com"
...
Connecting to www.example.com (www.example.com)|184.27.123.48|:443... connected.
HTTP request sent, awaiting response... 200 OK
Length: 1256 (1.2K) [text/html]
Saving to: ‘index.html’
...
Bash
.wget. will download the resource specified in the url to the current directory
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.  brew. .yum. .wget.
slides.notes:
Next, let’s see wget in action. The command is very simple — just type wget followed by the URL.
For example, here you can see we downloaded a web page from Lifewire using: wget "https://www.lifewire.com/uses-of-command-wget-2201085"
It then connects to the server, fetches the file, and saves it in the current directory. By default, the file will have the same name as the resource you are downloading.
This is super handy for downloading web pages, files, or even scripts without needing a browser.Practical

slides.title: Web Content
slides.body:
Downloading Files From Web
.curl. is a command-line utility for transferring data from or to a server designed to work without user interaction
$ sudo apt install curl 
Syntax
$ sudo brew install curl 
Syntax
$ sudo yum install curl 
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.  brew. .yum. .wget. .curl.
slides.notes:
Moving ahead, let’s talk about another very popular tool — curl. Unlike wget,which mainly downloads files, curl is much more versatile. It can transfer data to and from servers and works without any user interaction.
Before using it, we may need to install it. The installation depends on the system we’re using:
On Ubuntu/Debian, we use sudo apt install curl.
On MacOS, it’s brew install curl.
And for RedHat/CentOS, it’s sudo yum install curl.
Once installed, we’ll be able to use curl to interact with APIs, download content, or even send data to servers.

slides.title: Web Content
slides.body:
Downloading Files From Web
.curl. prints the contents of the URL to the output
$ curl "URL" 
Syntax
ib-developer@cloud:~$ curl "wttr.in"
Weather report: Hyderabad, India
                Haze
  _ - _ - _ - +28(26) °C     
   _ - _ - _  ← 0 km/h       
  _ - _ - _ - 4 km           
                0.0 mm
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.  brew. .yum. .wget. .curl.
slides.notes:
Now let’s actually see curl in action. Unlike wget, which saves the file to your system, curl prints the contents of the URL directly to the terminal output.
For example, if we run curl wttr.in, it shows us a weather report right inside the terminal. Here, it’s displaying the weather details for Hyderabad, including temperature, wind, and visibility.
So, curl is super handy not only for downloading files but also for quickly checking APIs or web services without needing a browser.


Practical

slides.title: Web Content
slides.body:
Removing a Package
remove: removes the installed packages
$ sudo apt remove package_name
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  apt.  brew. .yum. .wget. .curl.
slides.notes:
Next, let’s see how to remove a package. In Linux, if you no longer need a package, you can simply run sudo apt remove package_name. This will uninstall the package but keep the configuration files.
It’s useful when you want to free up space or clean up unnecessary software. PracticalNow one thing to not here is that we can search a package, update a package and add private repository, for these You can refer to the cheatsheet and practice.
